input.rationale: Decoded the rejected configuration entries by extending the rejection operand to include each ConfChangeV2's transition and change list, and the draft-side run answers the last open question about the mechanism. The log at the rejecting nodes is '1:t0 2:t2(tr=1,1:4) 3:t0 4:t2(tr=1,0:4)': index 2 is a joint-enter change that REMOVES node 4 (change type 1), index 4 is a joint-enter change that ADDS node 4 (change type 0), and neither is a leave-joint entry. So the committed history contains a joint configuration entered by a change that removes a non-member - a no-op change in terms of the voter set, since removing a node that is not present changes nothing - and then a second joint-enter change in the same configuration. The AutoLeave promise is what failed to break the cycle: appliedTo only proposes the leave when the applying node is the leader, so a joint change whose proposer is displaced before it applies the change leaves the cluster joint with nobody having proposed the leave, and the next leader's guard sees a non-joint tracker plus a stale pendingConfIndex and appends the second joint-enter change, which every node that applies the log in order then rejects. I request isolated execution so the decoded entries are receipt-backed before that account replaces the earlier, coarser explanation.

scope.description: One fixed harness with two sourced probes. Probe A (TestAssuranceCampaignWithUnappliedConfChange) covers the campaign admission guard: a voter built from MemoryStorage with entries [1]=normal and [2]=EntryConfChangeV2 at term 1, HardState.Commit=2 and Config.Applied=1, driven by MsgHup and by MsgTimeoutNow (term-carrying), then re-driven after raftLog.appliedTo(2,0); a control node has the same applied/committed gap but a normal entry at index 2. Probe B (TestAssuranceReadIndexAcrossTermChange) covers ReadOnlySafe completion across an authority change: elect a leader over a real 3-node in-process network, commit an entry in its term, admit a MsgReadIndex with no heartbeat responses delivered, then deliver a real higher-term campaign message from peer 2, and finally confirm a read admitted on the new leader with a single peer heartbeat response echoing the leader's context. Each case prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with the observed operands (state, term, vote, applied, committed, has_unapplied, unconfirmed_reads, confirmed_reads, read_states, vote targets, read index).
assumptions: Both probes use the snapshot's own test facilities (newTestRaft/newTestConfig/newTestMemoryStorage/withPeers/newNetwork) in one process.
Probe A's supplied state is a real MemoryStorage prefix plus a HardState and Config.Applied=1, so the applied<committed gap is produced by the application lag the field models.
Probe B's authority change is produced by a real peer campaigning over the in-process network, not by calling an internal transition.
No production logic is modified.

result.summary: Decoded the rejected configuration entries and the operands answer the last open question about the mechanism. The rejection operand now includes each ConfChangeV2's transition and change list, and the draft-side run shows the log at the rejecting nodes to be '1:t0 2:t2(tr=1,1:4) 3:t0 4:t2(tr=1,0:4)': index 2 is a joint-enter change that removes node 4, index 4 is a joint-enter change that adds node 4, and neither is a leave-joint entry. So the committed history enters a joint configuration with a change that removes a non-member (a no-op for the voter set) and then enters another joint configuration from within it. The AutoLeave promise is what fails to break that cycle: appliedTo proposes the leave-joint change only when the applying node is the leader, so a joint change whose proposer is displaced before it applies its own change leaves the cluster joint with nobody having proposed the leave, and the next leader's guard then sees a non-joint tracker plus a stale pendingConfIndex and appends the second joint-enter change, which every node applying the log in order subsequently rejects. This replaces the earlier, coarser explanation with one fitted to the decoded entries and consistent with the deterministic guard observation in the previous receipt. scope.description: Ninth revision of the same fixed harness; probes A, B and C are unchanged. The sweep adds application lag: the per-step persist/apply pass now skips a randomly chosen node about one time in six, so that node's applied index stays behind its committed index and a committed configuration change can remain unapplied there. The liveness witness then has its antecedent, and the summary reports unapplied_conf_change_states (how many check points had a node with a committed-but-unapplied configuration change) alongside stalled_states (how many of those had no promotable node), plus seeds, steps, elections, ordinary proposals, conf_change_proposals, restarts and violations; when the witness fires it also emits up to three liveness_witness events carrying per-node state, term, applied, committed, has_unapplied, promotable and in_config. Restart events now flush the node's committed entries to storage before recording its hard state, because a node with application lag can hold a committed index beyond its stored log and newRaft rejects such a hard state.
assumptions: Everything comes from the snapshot's own facilities (newTestRaft, newTestMemoryStorage, newNetwork, nextEnts, confChangeToMsg, applyConfChange, hasUnappliedConfChanges, promotable, newRaft, SetHardState); no production logic is modified.
Application lag is produced by not running the apply step for a node, which is what a slow or stalled application looks like to raft; the node's own log is still replicated normally.
The restart event is well formed by construction: entries are flushed before the hard state is recorded, so the restarted instance's commit index is within its stored log.
Randomness is fixed per seed; counts over a fixed seed set are descriptive, not rates.
